<reason>Side A won solidly by exposing a central contradiction in Side B's case and dismantling B's core economic warnings with realistic, proportional mechanisms. When B claimed both that clothing is forensically impossible for platforms to authenticate and that individual buyers are the "least-cost avoiders" who can verify items at home or hire third-party authenticators, A trapped B into conceding that buyers can only perform a basic "sanity check" against obvious fakes. Side A also neutralized B's warning that liability would destroy the vintage market by pointing out that counterfeiters target recognizable, high-demand labels rather than obscure vintage pieces, allowing platforms to target screening where fraud clusters while using payout clawbacks against scammers. Side B remained rhetorically polished but repeatedly strawmanned the motion as a mandate to physically inspect every $50 vintage tee.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's attack in [A2.1]-[A2.3] and follow-up in [A4.3]-[A4.5] exposing the contradiction between Side B's claim that garments cannot be forensically authenticated [B1.1] and its claim that solo buyers can verify items themselves or pay third-party authenticators to prove fraud [B1.5]-[B1.6], which forced B into a fatal concession in [B2.1].</best_rebuttal>
